lead: A nerve or muscle fires when its membrane is pushed past a threshold by charge. Electrotherapy passes a controlled current pulse through skin electrodes to do that on purpose. The same idea relieves pain (TENS), retrains a weak muscle (EMS/NMES), contracts a paralysed muscle (FES), or helps a surgeon find a motor nerve with a hand-held probe. The instrument is a pulse generator with a constant-current output; its dose is amplitude, pulse width and frequency.
prereq: You need the action potential, nerve conduction and EMG recording, and the current limits from electrical safety.

blocks.text: Tissue is an electrolyte. Current enters through a metal electrode, crosses skin, runs along nerve and muscle, and leaves through a return electrode. A nerve responds to the charge crossing its membrane in a short time, not to the average current over a minute. So the stimulator makes short pulses with a gap between them.

Four numbers describe the pulse. Amplitude is peak current, usually 0–100 mA for surface stimulation. Pulse width is how long one pulse lasts, usually 50–400 µs. Frequency is pulses per second, usually 1–150 Hz. Charge per pulse is amplitude × width.

blocks.where: Q is charge per pulse in coulombs (C); I is the set current in amperes (A); t is the pulse width in seconds (s).

blocks.text: A fifth number is the duty cycle: the fraction of time the current is on. With width t and frequency f, D = t × f, and average current is I × D. A 20 mA pulse of 200 µs at 100 Hz has only 0.4 mA average current, but the nerve sees the 20 mA peak. The peak excites; the average is safe for skin.

blocks.where: D is duty cycle (a fraction, no unit); t is pulse width in seconds (s); f is pulse frequency in hertz (Hz).

blocks.text: Electrodes are the other half of the circuit. Charge density = charge per pulse ÷ electrode area, in coulombs per square centimetre (C/cm²), or more conveniently microcoulombs per square centimetre (µC/cm²). For a biphasic pulse, use the charge of one phase. Too much charge density burns skin. Modern units use biphasic pulses — a positive pulse followed by an equal negative pulse — so net charge per cycle is zero and electrochemical damage is reduced.

TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) puts electrodes over the painful area or the nerve supplying it. It excites large sensory fibres (Aβ) that carry touch and pressure. Gate-control theory says their signals close a 'gate' in the spinal cord, so smaller pain fibres (Aδ and C) cannot pass theirs up. TENS relieves pain without a muscle contraction. Typical settings: 10–100 Hz, 50–200 µs, comfortable tingling.

EMS (electrical muscle stimulation) and NMES (neuromuscular electrical stimulation) act on motor nerves: the nerve fires and the muscle contracts. They re-educate a muscle after injury or surgery, when the patient cannot contract it voluntarily. FES (functional electrical stimulation) times the same pulses to a function, such as lifting a foot during walking in foot-drop, or cycling in spinal-cord injury.

Interferential therapy (IFT) uses two currents at about 4 kHz that differ by 1–150 Hz. They cross in tissue and produce a low-frequency beat at the difference frequency. The high carrier penetrates skin with less discomfort; the beat does the stimulation. Russian current is a 2.5 kHz sine wave switched on and off in bursts at 50 Hz — typically 10 ms on and 10 ms off, repeated 50 times a second, so the burst duty cycle is 50 %. It is used for muscle strengthening.

Older names are still asked. Galvanic current is steady direct current (DC), used for iontophoresis or wound healing. Faradic current is a short interrupted DC pulse that excites motor nerves. Both are less used now, but exams still compare them with TENS.

A stimulator has five blocks, shown in the figure. A battery powers an oscillator that sets the frequency (1–150 Hz). A pulse shaper sets the width (50–400 µs) and makes the pulse rectangular or biphasic. The output stage is a constant-current source: it changes its voltage to push the set current through the electrode–skin resistance, which varies from person to person and with sweat. Skin electrodes carry the current to the nerve or muscle.

A nerve stimulator for surgery is a hand-held probe with a fine tip. The surgeon touches it near a suspected motor nerve; a small current (often 0.5–2 mA) makes the muscle twitch. That identifies the nerve before it is cut or avoided. The return electrode is a large pad on the skin. The same probe can test a nerve after repair.

A surface stimulator for TENS or EMS is a small battery box with two or four channels, each with an independent amplitude control. Output is constant current up to about 100 mA into 500–1000 Ω. The pulse is usually biphasic and charge-balanced. The device limits charge per pulse and average current to keep skin safe; the safety limits are covered under electrical safety. Nerve conduction velocity measurement uses the same kind of stimulator, but it is a recording test, not therapy.

examples.question: A TENS unit is set to amplitude 20 mA, pulse width 200 µs and frequency 100 Hz. The pulse is rectangular and monophasic for this calculation. Find (a) charge per pulse, (b) charge delivered per second, (c) duty cycle, (d) average current and (e) the charge density under one 5 cm × 5 cm electrode. Give units.
steps: Convert to SI: I = 20 mA = 0.020 A. t = 200 µs = 2×10⁻⁴ s. f = 100 Hz.
Charge per pulse: Q = I × t = 0.020 × 2×10⁻⁴ = 4×10⁻⁶ C = 4 µC.
Pulses per second = 100. Charge per second = 4×10⁻⁶ × 100 = 4×10⁻⁴ C/s = 0.4 mC/s.
Average current: I × D = 0.020 × 0.02 = 4×10⁻⁴ A = 0.4 mA, which equals charge per second.
Charge density: electrode area = 5 cm × 5 cm = 25 cm², so 4 µC ÷ 25 cm² = 0.16 µC/cm² per pulse. A 1 cm² electrode carrying the same pulse would put 4 µC/cm² under it, 25 times more.
The nerve sees 20 mA for 200 µs; the long-term average is only 0.4 mA.
examples.answer: Charge per pulse = 4 µC, charge per second = 0.4 mC/s, duty cycle = 2 %, average current = 0.4 mA, charge density = 0.16 µC/cm².

traps: Confusing pulse frequency with the internal carrier: Russian current has a 2.5 kHz carrier in 50 Hz bursts; interferential therapy has a 4 kHz carrier with a 1–150 Hz beat.
Assuming more current is always better. Peak current excites the nerve, but charge density at the electrode decides whether skin burns.
Mixing TENS and EMS. TENS acts on sensory fibres for pain and normally causes no twitch; EMS acts on motor fibres to make a muscle contract.
Using mixed units in duty cycle. 200 µs × 100 Hz = 0.02, not 20. Convert width to seconds first.
Thinking nerve conduction velocity measurement is electrotherapy. It uses a stimulator, but it is a recording test.

quiz.q: Define pulse width and pulse frequency in electrotherapy.
quiz.a: Pulse width is the duration of one current pulse, typically 50–400 µs. Pulse frequency is the number of pulses per second, typically 1–150 Hz.

quiz.q: Why does a constant-current output matter when skin resistance changes?
quiz.a: Skin resistance changes with sweat, pressure and electrode contact. A constant-current source adjusts its output voltage so the set current stays the same. The charge per pulse (I × t) then stays fixed, so the dose does not drift.

quiz.q: A stimulator gives 40 mA, 100 µs, 50 Hz. Find charge per pulse, charge per second, duty cycle and average current.
A patient feels tingling and pain relief from TENS but no muscle twitch. Explain which nerve fibres are excited and why there is no twitch.
quiz.a: TENS excites large sensory Aβ fibres because the amplitude is set below the motor threshold, and the electrodes sit over the painful area or the supplying nerve rather than over the motor point. So no motor axon fires and no twitch appears. A twitch needs EMS amplitude and electrodes on the motor point.

quiz.q: Compare TENS and EMS by target and effect.
quiz.a: TENS targets sensory nerve fibres for pain relief; it does not normally cause a muscle contraction. EMS targets motor nerve fibres to make a muscle contract, used for muscle re-education or strengthening.

quiz.q: A Russian current has a 2.5 kHz carrier switched on for 10 ms in every 20 ms (50 Hz burst rate). Find the carrier period, the burst period, the number of carrier cycles in one burst and the burst duty cycle.
quiz.a: Carrier period = 1/2500 Hz = 0.4 ms. Burst period = 1/50 Hz = 20 ms. Cycles per burst = 10 ms ÷ 0.4 ms = 25 cycles. Burst duty cycle = 10 ms ÷ 20 ms = 0.5 = 50 %.

quiz.q: Why is a charge-balanced biphasic pulse safer for skin than a monophasic pulse of the same peak current?
quiz.a: A monophasic pulse leaves net charge at the electrode, which drives electrochemical reactions (pH change, metal ions) and burns skin. A biphasic pulse has equal positive and negative phases, so net charge per cycle is zero. The charge per phase still must be limited, but the tissue sees no DC build-up.

Two medium-frequency currents (about 4 kHz) with a small difference (1–150 Hz) cross in tissue; the beat at the difference frequency stimulates nerve and the high carrier penetrates skin with less discomfort.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer work pairs surface stimulation with machine learning that decodes intended movement from EMG, so FES timing becomes more natural. Wearable stimulators use flexible printed electrodes and Bluetooth control. Research on kilohertz-frequency alternating current explores blocking pain without tingling. Search terms: closed-loop FES, charge-balanced biphasic stimulation, interferential beat frequency.
